triage.name: Colorectal Cancer
triage.reason: Common malignancy with clear presentation of bleeding, weight loss, and anemia; diagnosis reachable by history, exam, and colonoscopy.

demographics: Incidence rises steadily with age; most cases are diagnosed after age 50
Slightly more common in men than women
Black adults in the US have higher incidence and mortality than other racial groups
Increasing incidence among adults younger than 50
More common in developed countries and in urban populations

risk_factors.text: Personal history of colorectal adenomas or prior colorectal cancer
Family history of colorectal cancer in a first-degree relative
Inherited syndromes such as Lynch syndrome or familial adenomatous polyposis
Long-standing inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis or Crohn disease) involving the colon
Heavy alcohol use (three or more drinks per day)
Diet high in red or processed meat and low in fiber, fruits, and vegetables

family_history: Colorectal cancer in a first-degree relative
Colorectal cancer diagnosed in a relative before age 50
Known Lynch syndrome or familial adenomatous polyposis in the family
Multiple family members with colorectal or other Lynch-associated cancers (endometrial, ovarian, gastric, urinary tract)
social_history: Low fiber intake with high red or processed meat consumption

chief_complaints.text: I've been seeing blood in my stool
My bowel habits have changed and won't go back to normal
I feel like I can't empty my bowels completely
My stomach has been cramping and bloated

hpi.onset: Gradual and insidious over weeks to months; often no symptoms at all early on
hpi.duration: Usually weeks to months by the time of diagnosis
hpi.progression: Symptoms are persistent and slowly worsen; bleeding may become more frequent, bowel changes become constant, and weight loss and fatigue progress
hpi.location: Lower abdomen or rectum; discomfort may be vague and poorly localized
hpi.quality: Blood in or on the stool; crampy, aching abdominal discomfort; a persistent urge to defecate
hpi.severity: Variable; often mild at first and easy to dismiss, becoming more bothersome as disease advances
hpi.timing: Bowel changes and bleeding are persistent rather than intermittent; rectal bleeding may occur with each bowel movement
relieving: Passing stool or gas temporarily relieves cramping
Nothing reliably relieves the bleeding or bowel change

associated_symptoms.text: Change in stool caliber (narrow, pencil-thin stools)
Iron-deficiency anemia found on blood work

pertinent_negatives: Bloody diarrhea with mucus and urgency suggesting acute infectious colitis
Severe constant abdominal pain with guarding or rebound
Vomiting of blood or coffee-ground material
Recent travel or antibiotic use preceding diarrhea
Known hemorrhoids only, with no change in bowel habits

positives.text: Blood in stool (bright red or dark)
Blood in urine (if tumor invades bladder)

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with vague symptoms attributed to aging, such as fatigue, anemia, or mild abdominal discomfort, without obvious bleeding or bowel change.
Colorectal cancer is very rare in children; when it occurs it is usually associated with an inherited syndrome and presents with abdominal pain, weight loss, or a palpable mass.
Symptoms such as rectal bleeding, anemia, and bowel changes are often attributed to pregnancy or hemorrhoids, delaying diagnosis.
missing_classic_features: Clear temporal separation from pregnancy-related symptoms

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with more aggressive disease or atypical symptoms due to underlying conditions or medications; bleeding and bowel changes may be attributed to infection or inflammation.

general.mild: Well-appearing, no distress; may look pale
general.moderate: Mildly pale and tired-appearing; comfortable at rest
general.severe: Pale, thin, chronically ill-appearing; may have temporal wasting
general.critical: Cachectic, pale, weak-appearing; may be in distress from obstruction or perforation

findings.maneuver: Inspect the conjunctivae and mucous membranes
Palpate all four quadrants of the abdomen
findings.finding: A palpable abdominal mass, most often in the right or left lower quadrant depending on tumor location
Abdominal distension with tympany suggesting obstruction

findings.maneuver: Palpate the liver edge below the right costal margin
Perform shifting dullness or fluid wave testing
Perform a digital rectal exam with a lubricated gloved finger
findings.finding: A palpable rectal mass or irregularity

findings.maneuver: Perform a digital rectal exam and inspect the glove for blood
findings.finding: Gross blood on the examining finger or in the rectal vault

findings.maneuver: Test a stool sample obtained on rectal exam for occult blood
Palpate the inguinal lymph node basins

findings.finding: Left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy (Virchow node) suggesting advanced disease

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen for masses and organomegaly
Assess for peritoneal signs with gentle palpation and cough
Inspect the perianal area and perform a digital rectal exam
findings.finding: No external hemorrhoids or fissure to explain bleeding

labs.caveat: Microcytic anemia from chronic blood loss; a normal hemoglobin does not rule out colorectal cancer, especially early disease.
Low MCV reflects iron deficiency from chronic occult blood loss.
Low ferritin confirms iron deficiency; ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and may be falsely normal with inflammation.
Reactive thrombocytosis from chronic inflammation or iron deficiency.
Low albumin reflects malnutrition or advanced disease and affects treatment planning.
Elevation suggests hepatobiliary involvement or hepatic metastases.
Rises with extensive hepatic replacement or biliary obstruction.
Elevated from dehydration, obstruction, or contrast exposure; guides chemotherapy dosing.
Hypercalcemia suggests bone metastases or paraneoplastic secretion.
Nonspecific marker of tumor burden or tissue turnover.
Negative. Required before cross-sectional imaging or systemic therapy in anyone who could be pregnant.

findings.finding: Sinus tachycardia from anemia, dehydration, or pain
Nonspecific ST-T changes from anemia or electrolyte disturbance

imaging.preferred_when: Patients who cannot or will not undergo colonoscopy

findings.text: Colonic mass or polyp detected on reconstructed images
Extracolonic findings such as hepatic lesions or lymphadenopathy

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV and oral contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Staging and evaluation for obstruction or metastases

findings.text: Colonic wall thickening or mass at the tumor site
Peritoneal nodules or ascites suggesting carcinomatosis

imaging.preferred_when: Local staging of rectal cancer and assessment of mesorectal fascia

findings.text: Rectal mass with depth of invasion through the bowel wall
Involvement of the mesorectal fascia or adjacent organs

imaging.preferred_when: Staging to evaluate for pulmonary metastases
Suspected recurrence or equivocal findings on conventional imaging

findings.text: FDG-avid primary tumor or metastatic lesions
Occult distant metastases not seen on CT

imaging.preferred_when: Diagnosis and biopsy of suspected colorectal cancer

findings.text: Visible mass, ulceration, or stricture in the colon or rectum

imaging.preferred_when: Limited evaluation of the distal colon when full colonoscopy is not possible

findings.text: Nonspecific; may show dilated bowel loops in obstruction

initial.why: Detects anemia from chronic blood loss and thrombocytosis
Assesses liver enzymes, albumin, and renal function before treatment
Rules out pregnancy before imaging or therapy
Direct visualization and biopsy of the suspected tumor

initial.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV and oral contrast
initial.why: Staging and evaluation for obstruction or metastases

supporting.why: Inflammatory marker that may reflect tumor burden

supporting.only_if: rectal cancer is suspected or confirmed
recurrence is suspected or conventional imaging is equivocal

supporting.why: Alternative when colonoscopy cannot be completed

not_indicated.why: Does not evaluate the proximal colon; colonoscopy is preferred
No role in the evaluation of colorectal cancer
Not needed unless pancreatitis is suspected
Not routinely helpful unless urinary symptoms suggest invasion

decision_points: Pregnancy test before CT or systemic therapy in anyone who could be pregnant
Colonoscopy with biopsy is required for histologic diagnosis before treatment
Staging with CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis (and pelvic MRI for rectal cancer) guides surgical and systemic therapy
Obstruction or perforation requires urgent surgical evaluation

differential.name: Hemorrhoidal disease
differential.why_considered: Bright red blood on the stool or toilet paper is the most common reason patients attribute rectal bleeding to hemorrhoids, and hemorrhoids are extremely common.

history: Bleeding is typically bright red, small in volume, and associated with straining or hard stools
No persistent change in bowel habits
No unintentional weight loss
Symptoms may be intermittent over years rather than progressive
exam: External hemorrhoids or skin tags visible on perianal inspection
labs: Hemoglobin and iron studies are usually normal
Fecal occult blood may be negative between episodes
imaging: Colonoscopy shows hemorrhoids but no mass or other source of bleeding

differential.name: Diverticular bleeding
differential.why_considered: Diverticular disease is a common cause of painless lower gastrointestinal bleeding in older adults, overlapping with the presentation of colorectal cancer.

history: Sudden, large-volume, painless bright red or maroon bleeding
Often resolves spontaneously
No change in bowel habits or weight loss between episodes
Known history of diverticulosis
exam: May show signs of acute blood loss if bleeding is brisk
labs: Acute drop in hemoglobin if bleeding is active
Iron studies may be normal if bleeding is recent rather than chronic
imaging: CT angiography or colonoscopy shows diverticula without a mass
Colonoscopy after bleeding stops may show diverticula as the only potential source

differential.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
differential.why_considered: Chronic bloody diarrhea, urgency, and abdominal cramping in ulcerative colitis or Crohn disease can mimic colorectal cancer, and long-standing colitis also raises cancer risk.

history: Younger age at onset, often with years of intermittent flares
Bloody diarrhea with mucus and urgency
Extra-intestinal symptoms such as joint pain, eye inflammation, or skin lesions
Symptoms fluctuate with flares rather than steadily progressing
exam: May be normal or show mild abdominal tenderness
Signs of chronic illness during severe flares
labs: Elevated inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR) during flares
Anemia may be present but iron deficiency is less prominent than in chronic occult cancer bleeding
Perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies or anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies may support the diagnosis
imaging: Colonoscopy shows continuous mucosal inflammation, friability, and pseudopolyps rather than a discrete mass
Biopsies show chronic inflammation and crypt architectural distortion, not adenocarcinoma

differential.name: Ischemic colitis
differential.why_considered: Older adults with vascular risk factors can present with abdominal pain and bloody stools, overlapping with colorectal cancer symptoms.

history: Sudden onset of crampy abdominal pain followed by urgency to defecate and then bloody diarrhea
Pain is often out of proportion to exam findings early on
Associated with atrial fibrillation, hypotension, or recent vascular events
Symptoms typically improve over days to weeks
exam: Mild to moderate abdominal tenderness over the affected segment
May have signs of hypoperfusion or arrhythmia
labs: Leukocytosis and elevated lactate may be present
Anemia is usually acute rather than chronic
imaging: CT shows segmental colonic wall thickening with pericolonic fat stranding
Colonoscopy shows segmental mucosal edema, erythema, or ulceration with a sharp transition
Biopsies show mucosal ischemia or ghost cells rather than adenocarcinoma

differential.name: Infectious colitis
differential.why_considered: Acute bloody diarrhea with abdominal cramping and fever can resemble the bowel changes and bleeding of colorectal cancer.

history: Acute onset over hours to days
Recent travel, antibiotic use, or consumption of undercooked food
Fever, tenesmus, and watery or bloody diarrhea
Sick contacts with similar symptoms
labs: Stool studies positive for a pathogen (e.g., Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, E. coli O157:H7, C. difficile toxin)
imaging: CT may show diffuse colonic wall thickening
Colonoscopy is usually avoided in acute infectious colitis due to perforation risk
Stool testing and clinical course establish the diagnosis

differential.name: Irritable bowel syndrome
differential.why_considered: Chronic abdominal pain with altered bowel habits is common in IBS and can be mistaken for the bowel changes of colorectal cancer, especially in younger patients.

history: Long-standing fluctuating symptoms, often years
Pain relieved by defecation and associated with changes in stool frequency or form
No rectal bleeding, weight loss, or anemia
Symptoms often triggered by stress or specific foods
exam: No mass, no blood on rectal exam
No signs of malnutrition or chronic illness
labs: Normal CBC, iron studies, and inflammatory markers
Celiac serology may be checked and is negative
imaging: Colonoscopy is normal or shows only benign findings

differential.name: Colonic obstruction from adhesions or stricture
differential.why_considered: Colorectal cancer can present with obstruction, and other causes of large bowel obstruction such as adhesions or benign strictures can mimic this presentation.

history: Prior abdominal or pelvic surgery suggesting adhesions
History of diverticulitis or inflammatory bowel disease suggesting benign stricture
Gradual onset of constipation, abdominal distension, and vomiting
No rectal bleeding or weight loss if benign
labs: Anemia and iron deficiency are less typical
imaging: CT shows a transition point without a mass or with a benign-appearing stricture
Colonoscopy or barium enema can distinguish a benign stricture from malignancy

differential.name: Lymphoma of the colon
differential.why_considered: Primary colonic lymphoma is rare but can present with abdominal pain, a palpable mass, weight loss, and anemia, mimicking colorectal adenocarcinoma.
differential.trigger: A colonic mass with B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss) or a mass that appears atypical on imaging

history: B symptoms such as fever, drenching night sweats, and significant weight loss
May have a known history of immunosuppression or inflammatory bowel disease
Symptoms may be more systemic than in typical colorectal cancer
exam: Generalized lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly may be present
labs: Cytopenias or atypical lymphocytes on CBC
Anemia may be present but iron deficiency is not the primary mechanism
imaging: CT shows a bulky, homogeneous colonic mass with regional or distant lymphadenopathy
PET-CT shows FDG avidity in the mass and nodes
Biopsy is required and shows lymphoid origin, not adenocarcinoma

severity.mild: Early, localized disease: small tumor confined to the bowel wall, no symptoms or only mild intermittent rectal bleeding, no anemia or weight loss
severity.moderate: Locally advanced disease: tumor invades through the bowel wall or involves regional lymph nodes, with persistent bleeding, change in bowel habits, and mild anemia
severity.severe: Advanced disease with significant anemia, weight loss, partial obstruction, or distant metastases; may require urgent intervention
severity.critical: Life-threatening complications such as complete bowel obstruction with perforation, massive hemorrhage, or sepsis

red_flags.finding: Unintentional weight loss with rectal bleeding
red_flags.meaning: Suggests malignancy and warrants urgent colonoscopy

red_flags.finding: Iron-deficiency anemia in a man or postmenopausal woman
red_flags.meaning: Colorectal cancer must be excluded until proven otherwise

red_flags.finding: New persistent change in bowel habits after age 45
Abdominal distension with vomiting and inability to pass stool or gas
red_flags.meaning: Possible bowel obstruction; needs urgent imaging and surgical evaluation

red_flags.finding: Severe abdominal pain with guarding or rebound
red_flags.meaning: Possible perforation and peritonitis; surgical emergency

red_flags.finding: Large-volume rectal bleeding with hypotension or tachycardia
red_flags.meaning: Hemodynamic instability from hemorrhage; resuscitate and evaluate urgently

complications.name: Bowel obstruction
clues: Inability to pass stool or gas

complications.name: Fistula formation to adjacent organs
clues: Pneumaturia or fecaluria if bladder involved
Passage of stool or gas per vagina

special_populations.differences: May present with vague symptoms such as fatigue, anemia, or mild abdominal discomfort without obvious bleeding or bowel change; higher rates of comorbidity affecting treatment tolerance.
Symptoms such as rectal bleeding, anemia, and bowel changes are often attributed to pregnancy or hemorrhoids, delaying diagnosis; imaging and treatment must account for fetal safety.
May present with more aggressive disease or atypical symptoms; bleeding and bowel changes may be attributed to infection or inflammation, delaying diagnosis.
Obesity is a risk factor and may complicate surgical approach and staging imaging; symptoms may be attributed to weight-related issues.
Type 2 diabetes is associated with increased risk; may present with atypical symptoms and higher rates of postoperative complications.

cancer.screening: The USPSTF recommends screening for colorectal cancer in all adults aged 45 to 75 years. For adults aged 76 to 85 years, screening should be individualized based on overall health, prior screening history, and patient preferences. Screening options include colonoscopy every 10 years, flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 years, CT colonography every 5 years, and stool-based tests such as annual high-sensitivity fecal occult blood testing or fecal immunochemical testing, and multi-target stool DNA testing every 1 to 3 years. Colonoscopy is preferred for individuals with a family history or other risk factors.
cancer.pathology: The vast majority of colorectal cancers are adenocarcinomas arising from adenomatous polyps or sessile serrated lesions. Other less common types include mucinous adenocarcinoma, signet ring cell carcinoma, medullary carcinoma, and neuroendocrine tumors. Molecular pathways include chromosomal instability, microsatellite instability (MSI), and CpG island methylator phenotype. Approximately 15% of colorectal cancers show MSI, which may be sporadic or associated with Lynch syndrome. Immunohistochemistry for mismatch repair proteins and testing for BRAF and KRAS mutations guide prognosis and therapy.
cancer.staging_concepts: Staging uses the TNM system. T describes depth of invasion through the bowel wall, N describes regional lymph node involvement, and M describes distant metastases. Stage I is confined to the bowel wall; stage II invades through the wall but has no nodal involvement; stage III involves regional lymph nodes; stage IV includes distant metastases. Staging is performed with CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, and pelvic MRI for rectal cancer. PET-CT may be used for equivocal findings. Serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is obtained at baseline and followed during treatment.

key_questions.question: Have you noticed blood in your stool or on the toilet paper?
key_questions.looking_for: Rectal bleeding, bright red or dark, persistent rather than a one-time episode

key_questions.question: Has there been any change in your bowel habits, and how long has it lasted?
key_questions.looking_for: Persistent change over more than a few days: new constipation, diarrhea, or alternating pattern

key_questions.question: Has your stool become narrower or a different shape than usual?
key_questions.looking_for: Pencil-thin or narrowed stools suggesting a distal obstructing lesion

key_questions.question: Do you feel like you cannot empty your bowels completely, or do you have to strain or go frequently?
key_questions.looking_for: Tenesmus and a sense of incomplete evacuation, typical of rectal tumors

key_questions.question: Have you lost weight without trying?
key_questions.looking_for: Unintentional weight loss, a red flag for malignancy

key_questions.question: Have you been more tired or short of breath than usual?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptoms of anemia from chronic occult blood loss

key_questions.question: Have you had cramping, bloating, gas pains, or a feeling of fullness?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent crampy abdominal discomfort or distension

key_questions.question: When was your last colonoscopy or colorectal cancer screening, and what were the results?
key_questions.looking_for: Never screened, overdue for screening, or prior adenomas/polyps removed

key_questions.question: Have you ever had colon polyps, colorectal cancer, or inflammatory bowel disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior adenomas, prior colorectal cancer, or long-standing ulcerative colitis or Crohn disease

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had colorectal cancer or polyps, and at what age?
key_questions.looking_for: First-degree relative with colorectal cancer, especially before age 50, or a known inherited syndrome

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had cancer of the uterus, ovary, stomach, or urinary tract?
key_questions.looking_for: Lynch syndrome-associated cancers suggesting a hereditary syndrome

key_questions.question: Do you smoke, drink alcohol, and how much?
key_questions.looking_for: Cigarette smoking, heavy alcohol use (three or more drinks per day)

key_questions.question: What does your diet look like, and how much do you exercise?
key_questions.looking_for: High red or processed meat intake, low fiber, sedentary lifestyle

key_questions.question: Have you had fever, night sweats, or bloody diarrhea with mucus and urgency?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests infectious colitis or inflammatory bowel disease rather than cancer

key_questions.question: Have you had vomiting, inability to pass stool or gas, or severe constant abdominal pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Obstruction or perforation requiring urgent surgical evaluation

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last menstrual period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy status before imaging or systemic therapy

reasoning_points: Age 45 or older with persistent rectal bleeding, a change in bowel habits, or unexplained iron-deficiency anemia
Unintentional weight loss and fatigue from chronic occult blood loss
Risk factors such as prior adenomas, family history of colorectal cancer, or long-standing inflammatory bowel disease
Iron-deficiency anemia with low MCV and low ferritin on laboratory testing
A palpable abdominal or rectal mass on examination, or gross blood on digital rectal exam
Colonoscopy with biopsy showing adenocarcinoma confirms the diagnosis
Staging with CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis (and pelvic MRI for rectal cancer) guides treatment

easy: Older adult with visible rectal bleeding, weight loss, and a change in bowel habits
Iron-deficiency anemia with low MCV and low ferritin
Palpable rectal mass or gross blood on digital rectal exam
Colonoscopy shows a mass and biopsy confirms adenocarcinoma
medium: Right-sided colon cancer presenting with fatigue and anemia but no visible bleeding
Symptoms attributed to hemorrhoids for months before evaluation
Normal hemoglobin with only a positive fecal occult blood test
Younger adult with a family history prompting earlier evaluation
hard: Older adult with vague fatigue and anemia attributed to aging
Pregnancy with rectal bleeding attributed to hemorrhoids
Presentation with obstruction or perforation rather than bleeding
Atypical colonic mass later found to be lymphoma rather than adenocarcinoma
